questions.stem: The atmosphere is 78% nitrogen gas (N2), yet plants cannot use nitrogen in this form. Why can plants not absorb nitrogen gas directly?

options.text: Plants do not need nitrogen for growth
Nitrogen gas molecules have a very strong triple bond that plants cannot break; plants can only absorb nitrogen as nitrates (NO3-) or ammonium (NH4+) dissolved in soil water
There is not enough nitrogen in the atmosphere for plants to use
Nitrogen gas is toxic to plant roots

questions.explanation: Atmospheric nitrogen (N2) has a very strong triple covalent bond between the two nitrogen atoms, which plants cannot break. Plants can only absorb nitrogen in soluble forms - mainly nitrate ions (NO3-) through their roots. Nitrogen must first be 'fixed' into these usable forms by nitrogen-fixing bacteria or lightning.

questions.stem: Leguminous plants (like peas, beans, and clover) have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Farmers often plant clover between crop rotations. Why is this practice beneficial?

options.text: Clover provides shade for the soil, preventing evaporation
The nitrogen-fixing bacteria in clover roots convert atmospheric N2 into ammonium, enriching the soil with nitrogen compounds that benefit the next crop
Clover roots break up compacted soil for better drainage
Clover attracts pollinators that help the next crop to grow

questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium) in the root nodules of legumes convert atmospheric N2 into ammonium (NH4+), which is then converted to nitrates in the soil. When the clover is ploughed back into the soil, these nitrogen compounds are released, naturally fertilising the soil for the next crop. This reduces the need for artificial nitrogen fertilisers.

questions.stem: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium (NH4+) into nitrites (NO2-) and then into nitrates (NO3-). These bacteria require oxygen. A farmer notices that waterlogged, anaerobic soil leads to poor crop growth. Using your knowledge of the nitrogen cycle, explain why.

options.text: Waterlogged soil is too cold for plants to grow
Without oxygen, nitrifying bacteria cannot convert ammonium to nitrates, and denitrifying bacteria thrive, converting nitrates back to nitrogen gas - both reducing available nitrogen for plants
Waterlogged soil contains too many nitrates, which are toxic to plants
Water prevents nitrogen-fixing bacteria from functioning

questions.explanation: In waterlogged (anaerobic) soil, nitrifying bacteria cannot function because they need oxygen for their reactions. Additionally, denitrifying bacteria thrive in anaerobic conditions and convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas (N2), which escapes into the atmosphere. Both processes reduce the amount of available nitrates in the soil, limiting plant growth.

questions.stem: When organisms die, decomposers break down their proteins and release ammonium into the soil. What is this process called, and why is it essential for the nitrogen cycle?

options.text: Nitrogen fixation; it converts N2 gas into ammonia
Denitrification; it returns nitrogen to the atmosphere
Decomposition/ammonification; it recycles nitrogen locked in organic molecules back into inorganic ammonium that can re-enter the soil nitrogen cycle
Nitrification; it converts ammonium into nitrates

questions.explanation: When decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down proteins in dead organisms and animal waste, they release ammonium (NH4+) into the soil. This process is called ammonification (or decomposition). It is essential because it recycles the nitrogen trapped in organic molecules, making it available for nitrifying bacteria to convert into nitrates that plants can absorb.

questions.stem: Excessive use of nitrogen fertilisers on farmland can cause eutrophication in nearby rivers and lakes. Which sequence correctly describes how eutrophication occurs?

options.text: Fertiliser enters water -> fish are directly poisoned -> plants die -> water clears

Fertiliser enters water -> algal bloom occurs -> algae block light, killing aquatic plants -> dead plants and algae are decomposed by bacteria -> bacteria use up dissolved oxygen -> fish and other organisms suffocate
Fertiliser enters water -> water becomes toxic -> all organisms die immediately
Fertiliser enters water -> plants grow excessively -> animals have more food -> biodiversity increases

questions.explanation: Eutrophication follows a specific sequence: excess nitrates wash into waterways, stimulating rapid algal growth (algal bloom). The algae block light, killing underwater plants. When the algae and plants die, decomposing bacteria multiply rapidly, consuming dissolved oxygen (biochemical oxygen demand increases). The resulting oxygen depletion kills fish and other aerobic organisms. This is a major environmental consequence of fertiliser overuse.
